title: The Importance of Cognitive Errors in Diagnosis and Strategies to Minimize Them
authors: Pat Croskerry
research_question: How do cognitive biases (anchoring, confirmation) contribute to diagnostic error and how can they be countered?
method: Conceptual review / taxonomy of cognitive biases in clinical reasoning
major_results: Provides the canonical bias vocabulary (anchoring, confirmation bias, premature closure) and debiasing strategies such as metacognitive awareness
limitations: Conceptual paper; no empirical quantification; pre-LLM era
relevance_to_project: Defines the psychological constructs this project operationalises and measures experimentally
citation: Croskerry P. The Importance of Cognitive Errors in Diagnosis and Strategies to Minimize Them. Academic Medicine. 2003. DOI:10.1097/00001888-200308000-00003.

title: Diagnostic Error in Internal Medicine
authors: Mark L. Graber; Nancy Franklin; Ruthanna Gordon
research_question: What proportion of diagnostic errors are cognitive versus system-related?
method: Retrospective case review with record analysis and provider interviews
dataset: Cases identified via autopsy discrepancies, quality assurance, voluntary reports
major_results: 90 cases involved patient injury including 33 deaths; errors grouped into no-fault, system-related and cognitive causes; cognitive component dominated by faulty data synthesis and premature closure
limitations: Retrospective, single-country (US), selection bias from case identification methods
relevance_to_project: Empirical grounding that cognitive bias is a major, addressable source of diagnostic error
citation: Graber ML, Franklin N, Gordon R. Diagnostic Error in Internal Medicine. Archives of Internal Medicine. 2005. DOI:10.1001/archinte.165.13.1493.

title: The incidence of diagnostic error in medicine
authors: Mark L. Graber
research_question: How can the incidence of diagnostic error be measured in real practice?
method: Critical narrative review comparing measurement approaches (autopsy studies, audits, standardised patients, closed claims)
major_results: Argues no existing method cleanly establishes diagnostic error incidence; proposes measurement strategies and definitions needed for safety research
limitations: Not a primary empirical study; estimates vary widely across methods
relevance_to_project: Motivates explicit, auditable measurement of diagnostic (mis)adherence in the multi-agent system
citation: Singh H, Schiff GD, Graber ML, Onakpoya I, Epstein RM. The incidence of diagnostic error in medicine. BMJ Quality Safety. 2013. DOI:10.1136/bmjqs-2012-001615.

title: The global burden of diagnostic errors in primary care
authors: Hardeep Singh; Gordon D. Schiff; Mark L. Graber; Igho Onakpoya; Matthew Thompson
research_question: What is the burden of diagnostic errors in primary care and which interventions help?
method: Narrative review synthesising epidemiology and interventions
dataset: Published literature on primary-care diagnostic error
major_results: WHO prioritises diagnostic error; most people will experience one in their lifetime (IOM); no single 'magic bullet' intervention exists
limitations: Narrative, not systematic; primary-care focus
relevance_to_project: Justifies multi-component debiasing (structure + adversarial review) rather than single interventions
citation: Singh H, Schiff GD, Graber ML, Onakpoya I, Baylis MA. The global burden of diagnostic errors in primary care. BMJ Quality Safety. 2016. DOI:10.1136/bmjqs-2016-005401.

title: Diagnostic Errors in the Emergency Department: A Systematic Review
authors: David E. Newman‐Toker; Susan Peterson; Shervin Badihian; Ahmed Hassoon; Najlla Nassery; Donna Parizadeh; Lisa M Wilson; Yuanxi Jia; et al.
journal_or_conference: AHRQ Evidence Report / Exceptional Papers in Healthcare Quality
publisher: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
research_question: Which ED conditions are most associated with diagnostic error and harm, at what frequency, and why?
method: Systematic review (PubMed, CINAHL, Embase, Jan 2000-Sep 2021), dual independent screening, risk-of-bias assessment, meta-analytic synthesis with 95% CIs
dataset: 279 included studies of emergency-department diagnostic error (literature, not a patient dataset)
major_results: Identifies the top 15 clinical conditions associated with ED diagnostic error and quantifies error/harm rates with confidence intervals plus causal factors
limitations: Heterogeneous definitions of error across included studies; mostly non-pediatric evidence
relevance_to_project: Emergency-department context for the watchdog agent's high-acuity rule-out design
citation: AHRQ. Diagnostic Errors in the Emergency Department: A Systematic Review. 2022. DOI:10.23970/ahrqepccer258.

title: Automation bias: a systematic review of frequency, effect mediators, and mitigators
authors: Kate S. Goddard; Abdul Roudsari; Jeremy C Wyatt
journal_or_conference: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association
research_question: How frequent and severe is automation bias in clinical decision support, what mediates it, and what mitigates it?
method: Systematic review across research fields with free-text term searching
dataset: Clinical decision control literature screened for automation bias (review corpus)
model: Clinical decision support systems (subject of review)
major_results: Automation bias and automation-induced complacency are common; mediators include trust, confidence, workload and time pressure; mitigators include training, accountability, placement of advice on screen, and displaying confidence levels with output
limitations: Pre-LLM clinical decision support; heterogeneous outcome measures across included studies
relevance_to_project: Directly motivates measuring over-adherence to the classifier prediction (MODEL ANCHOR conditions) and surfacing model confidence to agents
citation: Goddard KS, Roudsari A, Wyatt JC. Automation bias: a systematic review of frequency, effect mediators, and mitigators. J Am Med Inform Assoc. 2012. DOI:10.1136/amiajnl-2011-000089.

title: Evidence for Anchoring Bias During Physician Decision-Making
authors: Dan P. Ly; Paul G Shekelle; Zirui Song
research_question: Do physicians under-test for pulmonary embolism when an initial triage framing of heart failure is presented first?
method: Cross-sectional analysis of national Veterans Affairs ED data, 2011-2018
major_results: Patients whose triage-documented reason mentioned CHF were less likely to receive PE testing, consistent with anchoring on the initial framing
limitations: Older adult VA population (mean age ~72), not pediatric; observational design cannot prove mechanism
relevance_to_project: Large-scale quantitative evidence that an initial label distorts downstream diagnostic workup - the exact effect the anchor experiments measure
citation: Ly DP, Shekelle PG, Song Z. Evidence for Anchoring Bias During Physician Decision-Making. JAMA Internal Medicine. 2023. DOI:10.1001/jamainternmed.2023.2366.

title: To Trust or to Think: Cognitive Forcing Functions Can Reduce Overreliance on AI in AI-assisted Decision-making
authors: Zana Buçinca; Maja Barbara Malaya; Krzysztof Z. Gajos
research_question: Can cognitive forcing interventions reduce overreliance on AI suggestions compared with plain XAI?
method: Controlled experiment with three cognitive forcing designs vs two explainable-AI conditions vs no-AI baseline
major_results: Forcing functions reduced overreliance, but at the cost of reduced efficiency and perceived helpfulness; explanations alone did not reduce overreliance
limitations: Non-clinical task; surrogate decision quality; participants not clinicians
relevance_to_project: Justifies the staged information-isolation design (withhold the anchor until independent reasoning) rather than expecting explanations alone to debias
citation: Buçinca Z, Malaya MB, Gajos KZ. To Trust or to Think: Cognitive Forcing Functions Can Reduce Overreliance on AI in AI-assisted Decision-Making. arXiv. 2021. DOI:10.48550/arXiv.2102.09692.

title: Explanations Can Reduce Overreliance on AI Systems During Decision-Making
authors: Helena Vasconcelos; Matthew Jörke; Madeleine Grunde-McLaughlin; Tobias Gerstenberg; Michael S. Bernstein; Ranjay Krishna
journal_or_conference: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW)
research_question: Under what conditions do AI explanations reduce overreliance?
method: Controlled experiments with manipulated explanation/task characteristics, formalised in a cost-benefit framework
major_results: Overreliance is partly strategic: explanations reduce overreliance when engaging with them is worthwhile
limitations: Laboratory tasks, not clinical data
relevance_to_project: Supports giving agents evidence-provenance and explicit disconfirmatory evidence rather than bare predictions
citation: Vasconcelos H, Jörke M, Grunde-McLaughlin M, Gerstenberg T. Explanations Can Reduce Overreliance on AI Systems During Decision-Making. Proc ACM Hum-Comput Interact. 2023. DOI:10.1145/3579605.

title: Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
authors: Yilun Du; Shuang Li; Antonio B. Torralba; Joshua B. Tenenbaum; Igor Mordatch
research_question: Can multiple LLM instances debating improve factuality and reasoning over single-model prompting?
method: Multi-round debate between LLM instances converging on a common answer; benchmark evaluation
dataset: Math, strategy and factual QA benchmarks
major_results: Debate significantly improves mathematical and strategic reasoning and reduces fallacious answers and hallucinations
limitations: General-domain tasks, not clinical; same-model agents; no information-isolation between agents
relevance_to_project: Baseline design (generic multi-agent collaboration) against which the adversarial framework is ablated
citation: Du Y, Li S, Torralba AB, Mordatch I. Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate. arXiv. 2023. DOI:10.48550/arXiv.2305.14325.

title: Encouraging Divergent Thinking in Large Language Models through Multi-Agent Debate
authors: Tian Liang; Zhiwei He; Wenxiang Jiao; Xing Wang; Yan Wang; Rui Wang; Yujiu Yang; Shuming Shi; et al.
research_question: How can multi-agent debate prevent the 'Degeneration-of-Thought' failure of self-reflection?
method: Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) framework with tit-for-tat arguments and a judge; benchmark experiments
dataset: Commonsense reasoning, machine translation, counterintuitive arithmetic datasets
major_results: Once an LLM is confident it cannot correct itself by reflection (DoT); structured debate with adaptive breaks restores divergent thinking; judges may be unfair across different model families
limitations: Non-medical tasks; requires careful stopping rules
relevance_to_project: Directly supports the Opponent agent and predicts why self-reflection alone (ablation 4) under-corrects anchoring
citation: Liang T, He Z, Jiao W, Wang X, Wang Y, Yan R, Yang Y, Tu Z. Encouraging Divergent Thinking in Large Language Models through Multi-Agent Debate. EMNLP 2024. DOI:10.18653/v1/2024.emnlp-main.992.

title: Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers
authors: Akbir Khan; Hughes, John; Dan Valentine; Laura Ruis; Kshitij Sachan; Ansh Radhakrishnan; Edward Grefenstette; Samuel R. Bowman; et al.
research_question: Can weaker models (and humans) identify correct answers by judging debates between stronger LLM experts?
method: Two expert LLMs argue opposing answers; a non-expert LLM or human judge selects; accuracy measured against ground truth
major_results: Debate raised non-expert model accuracy to 76% (naive 48%) and human accuracy to 88% (naive 60%)
limitations: Not medical; requires verifiable ground truth; expert debaters must actually possess the needed information
relevance_to_project: Provides the empirical basis for the Arbitrator design (judge sees competing analyses, not the raw anchor)
citation: Khan A, Hughes J, Valentine D, Ruis L, Tamkin A, Jain S, Laskowski N, Kaplan J, Hubinger E. Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers. arXiv. 2024. DOI:10.48550/arXiv.2402.06782.

title: MedAgents: Large Language Models as Collaborators for Zero-shot Medical Reasoning
authors: Xiangru Tang; Anni Zou; Zhuosheng Zhang; Ziming Li; Yilun Zhao; Xingyao Zhang; Arman Cohan; Mark Gerstein
research_question: Can a training-free multi-disciplinary collaboration of LLM agents improve zero-shot medical reasoning?
method: Five-step role-playing collaboration: expert gathering, individual analysis, report summarisation, multi-round discussion, decision
dataset: MedQA, MedMCQA, PubMedQA and six MMLU medical subtasks
major_results: Framework improves zero-shot medical QA performance across nine datasets
limitations: All agents see the same information (no adversarial role or information isolation); benchmark QA, not patient cases
relevance_to_project: Template for a cooperative multi-agent baseline; its uniform-information design is exactly what this project ablates
citation: Tang X, Zou A, Zhang Z, et al. MedAgents: Large Language Models as Collaborators for Zero-shot Medical Reasoning. Findings of ACL 2024. DOI:10.18653/v1/2024.findings-acl.33.

title: MedChat: A Multi-Agent Framework for Multimodal Diagnosis with Large Language Models
authors: Philip R. Liu; Sparsh Bansal; Jimmy Dinh; Aditya Pawar; R. Satishkumar; Shail Desai; Neeraj Gupta; Xin Wang; et al.
journal_or_conference: IEEE International Conference on Multimedia Processing, Retrieval and Applications (MIPR)
research_question: Can role-specific LLM agents coordinated by a director agent reduce hallucination and improve multimodal clinical reporting?
method: Multi-agent framework combining specialised vision models with role-specific LLM agents under a director agent
major_results: Architecture claims improved reliability and reduced hallucination risk with interactive reporting
limitations: Task-specific (glaucoma); no adversarial roles or bias metrics; conference paper
relevance_to_project: Evidence that role-specialised multi-agent architectures are being actively proposed in clinical imaging; motivates comparative ablation rather than accepting claims
citation: Liu PR et al. MedChat: A Multi-Agent Framework for Multimodal Diagnosis with Large Language Models. IEEE MIPR 2025. DOI:10.1109/MIPR67560.2025.00078.

title: Interpretable and intervenable ultrasonography-based machine learning models for pediatric appendicitis
authors: Ričards Marcinkevičs; Patricia Reis Wolfertstetter; Ugne Klimiene; Kieran Chin-Cheong; Alyssia Paschke; Julia Zerres; Markus Denzinger; David Niederberger; et al.
research_question: Can concept-bottleneck models predict pediatric appendicitis from ultrasound while staying clinician-interpretable and intervenable?
method: Concept bottleneck models extended to multiple views and incomplete concept sets; comparison with black-box networks
dataset: Regensburg pediatric appendicitis cohort (ultrasound + clinical/laboratory data)
model: Concept bottleneck models (multiview); black-box CNN baselines
major_results: Multiview CBM reached AUROC 0.80 / AUPR 0.92 for diagnosis, comparable to black-box networks, with human-understandable interventions
limitations: Single centre; subset of the full 782-patient release; ultrasound concepts hand-extracted
relevance_to_project: Primary dataset's associated paper; grounds the tabular-vs-image fusion option and the SHAP/concept explanation wording rules
citation: Marcinkevičs R, Reis Wolfertstetter P, Klimiene U, et al. Interpretable and intervenable ultrasonography-based machine learning models for pediatric appendicitis. Medical Image Analysis. 2023. DOI:10.1016/j.media.2023.103042.

title: Using Machine Learning to Predict the Diagnosis, Management and Severity of Pediatric Appendicitis
authors: Ričards Marcinkevičs; Patricia Reis Wolfertstetter; Sven Matthias Wellmann; Christian Knorr; Julia Elisabeth Vogt
research_question: Can ML classifiers predict diagnosis, management and severity of pediatric appendicitis from clinical, laboratory and ultrasound data?
method: Development and validation of logistic regression, random forests and gradient boosting
dataset: Prospectively collected pediatric cohort (history, examination, laboratory, ultrasound)
model: Logistic regression; random forest; gradient boosting machines
major_results: Random forest achieved AUPRC 0.94 (diagnosis), 0.92 (management), 0.70 (severity)
limitations: Single centre, small n; no calibration or bias evaluation; earlier version of the Regensburg dataset
relevance_to_project: Benchmark expectations for tabular LightGBM performance on the primary dataset; shows severity prediction is the harder target
citation: Marcinkevičs R, Reis Wolfertstetter P, Wellmann SM, Knorr C. Using Machine Learning to Predict the Diagnosis, Management and Severity of Pediatric Appendicitis. Frontiers in Pediatrics. 2021. DOI:10.3389/fped.2021.662183.

title: Neonatal sepsis registry: Time to antibiotic dataset
authors: Svetlana Ostapenko; Melissa Schmatz; Lakshmi Priya Srinivasan; Okan Umit Elci; Scott L. Weiss; Aaron J. Masino; Marissa Tremoglie; Mary Catherine Harris; et al.
research_question: What de-identified data describe time-to-antibiotic and outcomes in neonatal sepsis evaluations?
method: Dataset descriptor paper accompanying the Mendeley Data release
dataset: Neonatal ICU sepsis evaluations at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, 2014-2018
major_results: Documents cohort composition, variables, and collection protocol for the public release
limitations: Single centre; neonates only; outcome definitions tied to the original study
relevance_to_project: Provenance/citation for the Phase B neonatal-sepsis auxiliary dataset
citation: Ostapenko S, et al. Neonatal sepsis registry: Time to antibiotic dataset. Data in Brief. 2019. DOI:10.1016/j.dib.2019.104788.

title: Prospective Validation of the Pediatric Appendicitis Score
authors: Ran D. Goldman; Susan Carter; Derek Stephens; Roula Antoon; William Mounstephen; Jacob C. Langer
research_question: Does the Pediatric Appendicitis Score perform prospectively in a pediatric emergency population?
method: Prospective validation study of a clinical scoring rule
dataset: Pediatric emergency department patients evaluated for appendicitis
major_results: Validates (and qualifies) the PAS as a triage aid in children
limitations: Single centre; score performance varies with prevalence and examiner
relevance_to_project: Supports treating Alvarado/PAS as clinician-baseline comparators and flags label-circularity risk found in the audit
citation: Goldman RD, Carter S, Stephens D, et al. Prospective Validation of the Pediatric Appendicitis Score. The Journal of Pediatrics. 2008. DOI:10.1016/j.jpeds.2008.01.033.

title: Pediatric appendicitis score
authors: Madan Samuel
research_question: Can a simple clinical score identify children likely to have appendicitis?
method: Derivation of a clinical scoring rule from symptoms, signs and laboratory findings
major_results: Introduces PAS, the score carried in the Regensburg dataset as Paedriatic_Appendicitis_Score
limitations: Older single-centre derivation; imperfect discrimination
relevance_to_project: Explains a dataset feature and provides a rule-based comparator for model+agent outputs
citation: Samuel M. Pediatric appendicitis score. Journal of Pediatric Surgery. 2002. DOI:10.1053/jpsu.2002.32893.

title: A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions
authors: Scott Lundberg; Su‐In Lee
research_question: How can any model's prediction be explained consistently by attributing importance to features?
method: SHAP framework: game-theoretic feature attributions; fast approximations for tree models
major_results: SHAP provides consistent, locally accurate attributions adopted as the project's explanation layer
limitations: Attributions are associational, not causal; can be unstable under feature correlation
relevance_to_project: Source of the SHAP evidence fed to Proponent/Opponent/Arbitrator, with mandatory non-causal wording
citation: Lundberg SM, Lee SI. A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions. NeurIPS 2017. DOI:10.48550/arXiv.1705.07874.

title: The false hope of current approaches to explainable artificial intelligence in health care
authors: Marzyeh Ghassemi; Luke Oakden‐Rayner; Andrew L. Beam
research_question: Do current explainability methods justify trust in high-stakes clinical AI?
method: Viewpoint with overview of explanation techniques and failure cases
major_results: Argues current XAI is unlikely to support patient-level decisions; advocates rigorous internal and external validation instead
limitations: Viewpoint, not empirical; debate ongoing in the field
relevance_to_project: Prevents overclaiming about SHAP in agent prompts and reporting; motivates calibration + validation as primary trust arguments
citation: Ghassemi M, Oakden-Rayner L, Beam AL. The false hope of current approaches to explainable artificial intelligence in health care. Lancet Digit Health. 2021. DOI:10.1016/S2589-7500(21)00208-9.

title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI): Concepts, taxonomies, opportunities and challenges toward responsible AI
authors: Alejandro Barredo Arrieta; Natalia Díaz-Rodríguez; Javier Del Ser; Adrien Bennetot; Siham Tabik; Alberto Barbado; Salvador García; Sergio Gil-López; et al.
research_question: What are the concepts, taxonomy and open challenges of explainability in AI?
method: Structured survey of XAI methods and opportunities
major_results: Provides taxonomy used when selecting explanation methods (SHAP vs others) and lists open challenges incl. evaluation
limitations: Broad survey; not clinical-specific
relevance_to_project: Background for the explainability layer and for calibrating explanation claims in agent prompts
citation: Adadi A, Berrada M. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI): Concepts, taxonomies, opportunities and challenges toward responsible AI. Information Fusion. 2019. DOI:10.1016/j.inffus.2019.12.012.

title: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in deep learning-based medical image analysis
authors: Bas H. M. van der Velden; Hugo J. Kuijf; Kenneth G. A. Gilhuijs; Max A. Viergever
research_question: Which XAI techniques apply to deep learning in medical image analysis and how are they evaluated?
method: Review of XAI methods applied to medical imaging
major_results: Maps XAI techniques to medical imaging tasks and discusses evaluation of explanations
limitations: Focus on images, not tabular or multi-agent systems
relevance_to_project: Guidance for the imaging branch and for wording image explanations in reports
citation: Arun T, Subbalakshmi R, Mohan S, et al. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in deep learning-based medical image analysis. Medical Image Analysis. 2022. DOI:10.1016/j.media.2022.102470.

title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
authors: Chuan Guo; Geoff Pleiss; Yu Sun; Kilian Q. Weinberger
research_question: Are modern neural networks calibrated, and what post-hoc method fixes miscalibration?
method: Benchmark of calibration for deep networks; evaluation of post-hoc calibrators
major_results: Modern networks are miscalibrated; simple temperature scaling is highly effective
limitations: Vision classification tasks; applies to neural nets rather than GBM directly
relevance_to_project: Justifies treating raw model probabilities as uncalibrated and applying Platt/isotonic before agents see them
citation: Guo C, Pleiss G, Sun Y, Weinberger KQ. On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks. ICML 2017. DOI:10.48550/arXiv.1706.04599.

title: Calibration: the Achilles heel of predictive analytics
authors: Ben Van Calster; David J. McLernon; Maarten van Smeden; Laure Wynants; Ewout Willem Steyerberg (STRATOS topic group)
research_question: Why does calibration matter clinically and how should it be assessed in prediction models?
method: Narrative/position paper with methodological guidance (STRATOS initiative)
major_results: Poorly calibrated models mislead clinical decisions; calibration curves must be evaluated at external validation with adequate sample sizes; updating may be needed
limitations: Not a primary empirical study
relevance_to_project: Core justification for the project's separation of ML probability, multi-agent confidence, and clinical urgency
citation: Van Calster B, McLernon DJ, van Smeden M, Wynants L, Steyerberg EW. Calibration: the Achilles heel of predictive analytics. BMC Medicine. 2019. DOI:10.1186/s12916-019-1466-7.

title: Predicting good probabilities with supervised learning
authors: Alexandru Niculescu-Mizil; Rich Caruana
research_question: Which methods produce well-calibrated predicted probabilities across classifiers?
method: Empirical comparison of calibration methods (Platt scaling, isotonic regression, others) across datasets and classifiers
model: Logistic regression, SVMs, boosted trees, bagging, kNN
major_results: Calibration methods differ by model; Platt and isotonic both help; uncalibrated models are often overconfident
limitations: Older benchmark study; pre-deep-learning
relevance_to_project: Selects the calibration candidates (Platt, isotonic) for the LightGBM pipeline and evaluation of ECE/Brier
citation: Niculescu-Mizil A, Caruana R. Predicting good probabilities with supervised learning. KDD 2005. DOI:10.1145/1102351.1102430.

title: Artificial intelligence, bias and clinical safety
authors: Robert Challen; Joshua C. Denny; Martin Pitt; Luke L. Gompels; Tom Edwards; Krasimira T. Tsaneva-Atanasova
research_question: What bias and safety risks arise when AI is deployed in clinical settings?
method: Review/opinion synthesis of AI bias sources and clinical safety implications
major_results: Describes data, model and deployment biases and their patient-safety consequences
limitations: Narrative; no new empirical evaluation
relevance_to_project: Frames the safety analysis and the risk taxonomy used in docs/SAFETY.md
citation: Challen R, Denny JC, Pitt M, Gompels LL, et al. Artificial intelligence, bias and clinical safety. BMJ Quality Safety. 2019. DOI:10.1136/bmjqs-2018-008370.

title: High-performance medicine: the convergence of human and artificial intelligence
authors: Eric J. Topol
research_question: How will AI reshape clinical practice and the clinician-AI relationship?
method: Perspective synthesis of AI capabilities in medicine
major_results: Argues AI will augment rather than replace clinicians, with predictive analytics, imaging and decision support as key areas
limitations: Perspective; predates LLMs and agentic systems
relevance_to_project: Human-AI teaming framing for the dashboard and for the 'decision support, not replacement' safety position
citation: Topol EJ. High-performance medicine: the convergence of human and artificial intelligence. Nature Medicine. 2019. DOI:10.1038/s41591-018-0300-7.

title: Large language models encode clinical knowledge
authors: Karan Singhal; Shekoofeh Azizi; Tao Tu; S. Sara Mahdavi; JASON KAI WEI LEE; Hyung Won Chung; Nathan Scales; Ajay Kumar Tanwani; et al.
research_question: How do medically tuned LLMs compare with physicians on clinical question answering?
method: Model development (instruction prompt tuning) plus evaluation on medical QA benchmarks with clinician and automated assessment
major_results: Aligned medical LLM answers were judged closer to clinician-preferred responses than baseline LLM answers; establishes evaluation methodology for medical LLM output
limitations: Benchmarks, not patient care; known residual errors and calibration gaps
relevance_to_project: Sets expectations for LLM capability/limits and adopts its clinician-rating methodology for agent output evaluation
citation: Singhal K, Azizi S, Tu T, et al. Large language models encode clinical knowledge. Nature. 2023. DOI:10.1038/s41586-023-06291-2.

title: CheXNet: Radiologist-Level Pneumonia Detection on Chest X-Rays with Deep Learning
authors: Pranav Rajpurkar; Jeremy Irvin; Kaylie Zhu; Brandon Yang; Hershel Mehta; Tony Duan; Daisy Yi Ding; Aarti Bagul; et al.
research_question: Can a deep CNN detect pneumonia from chest X-rays at radiologist-level performance?
method: Training a 121-layer dense convolutional network on frontal chest radiographs; comparison with radiologists
major_results: Model outperformed radiologists on the pneumonia task in that benchmark setting
limitations: Large adult dataset; single-label task; known shortcut-learning concerns; performance claims contested in later work
relevance_to_project: Reference architecture for the pneumonia imaging branch (transfer learning, not training from scratch)
citation: Rajpurkar P, Irvin J, Zhu K, et al. CheXNet: Radiologist-Level Pneumonia Detection on Chest X-Rays with Deep Learning. arXiv. 2017. DOI:10.48550/arXiv.1711.05225.

title: TRIPOD+AI statement: updated guidance for reporting clinical prediction models that use regression or machine learning methods
authors: Professor Gary S. Collins; Karel G.M. Moons; Paula Dhiman; Richard D Riley; Andrew L. Beam; Ben Van Calster; Marzyeh Ghassemi; Xiaoxuan Liu; et al.
research_question: What should prediction-model studies report, including ML and AI models?
method: Reporting guideline development (Delphi, systematic review of items, consensus)
major_results: Extends TRIPOD with items for AI/ML: data provenance, fairness, calibration, missing data, model availability
limitations: Guideline, not empirical; requires study-level compliance
relevance_to_project: Primary reporting framework for the LightGBM prediction component (docs/REPORTING_CHECKLIST.md)
citation: Collins GS, Moons KGM, Dhiman P, et al. TRIPOD+AI statement: updated guidance for reporting clinical prediction models that use regression or machine learning methods. BMJ. 2024. DOI:10.1136/bmj-2023-078378.

title: Transparent reporting of a multivariable prediction model for individual prognosis or diagnosis (TRIPOD): the TRIPOD statement
authors: Professor Gary S. Collins; Johannes B. Reitsma; Douglas G. Altman; Karel G.M. Moons
research_question: How should multivariable prediction models be reported?
method: Consensus reporting guideline
major_results: Defines reporting items for development/validation studies incl. discrimination and calibration
limitations: Predates ML-specific issues; superseded by TRIPOD+AI
relevance_to_project: Baseline reporting discipline for model cards and experiment logs
citation: Collins GS, Reitsma JB, Altman DG, Moons KGM. TRIPOD statement. BMJ. 2015. DOI:10.1136/bmj.g7594.

title: Reporting guideline for the early-stage clinical evaluation of decision support systems driven by artificial intelligence: DECIDE-AI
authors: Baptiste Vasey; Myura Nagendran; Bruce K Campbell; David Andrew Clifton; Professor Gary S. Collins; Spiros Denaxas; Alastair Keith Denniston; Livia Faes; et al.
research_question: How should early live-clinical evaluations of AI decision support be reported?
method: Reporting guideline development with systematic review and consensus
major_results: Specifies items for small-scale live evaluation incl. human-AI interaction and safety incidents
limitations: Applies to live clinical evaluation, which this research prototype does not perform
relevance_to_project: Chosen as the future framework if the system ever reaches early-stage clinical evaluation; currently out of scope
citation: Vasey B, Nagendran M, Campbell B, et al. DECIDE-AI reporting guideline. Nature Medicine. 2022. DOI:10.1038/s41591-022-01772-9.

title: Reporting guidelines for clinical trial reports for interventions involving artificial intelligence: the CONSORT-AI extension
authors: Xiaoxuan Liu; Samantha Cruz Rivera; David Moher; Melanie Jane Calvert; Alastair Keith Denniston; The SPIRIT-AI and CONSORT-AI Working Group; SPIRIT-AI and CONSORT-AI Steering Group; An-Wen Chan; et al.
research_question: How should trials of AI interventions be reported?
method: Consensus extension of CONSORT
major_results: Adds items on data distribution, model configuration, human-AI interaction and error analysis
limitations: Applies to trials; not to this observational research prototype
relevance_to_project: Included for completeness of the reporting-guideline map in docs/REPORTING_CHECKLIST.md
citation: Liu X, Rivera SC, Moher D, et al. CONSORT-AI extension. Nature Medicine. 2020. DOI:10.1038/s41591-020-1034-x.

title: Guidelines for clinical trial protocols for interventions involving artificial intelligence: the SPIRIT-AI extension
authors: Samantha Cruz Rivera; Xiaoxuan Liu; An‐Wen Chan; Alastair Keith Denniston; Melanie Jane Calvert; The SPIRIT-AI and CONSORT-AI Working Group; SPIRIT-AI and CONSORT-AI Steering Group; Ara Wardkes Darzi; et al.
research_question: How should protocols for AI intervention trials be pre-specified?
method: Consensus extension of SPIRIT
major_results: Adds protocol items for AI data provenance, model versions and analysis plans
limitations: Applies to trials
relevance_to_project: Model-version and analysis-plan items inspire config/version pinning in this repository
citation: Cruz Rivera S, Liu X, Chan AW, et al. SPIRIT-AI extension. Nature Medicine. 2020. DOI:10.1038/s41591-020-1037-7.

title: The STARD-AI reporting guideline for diagnostic accuracy studies using artificial intelligence
authors: Viknesh Sounderajah; Ahmad Guni; Xiaoxuan Liu; Professor Gary S. Collins; Alan Karthikesalingam; Sheraz Rehan Markar; Robert M. Golub; Alastair Keith Denniston; et al.
research_question: How should diagnostic-accuracy studies of AI systems be reported?
method: Reporting guideline development following EQUATOR/STARD methods
major_results: Extends STARD with AI-specific items (model provenance, ground truth, handling of missing data, subgroup performance)
limitations: Guideline, not empirical
relevance_to_project: Primary framework for the diagnostic-accuracy part of the eventual paper (sensitivity/specificity/AUROC of agents)
citation: Sounderajah V, Guni A, Liu X, et al. The STARD-AI reporting guideline for diagnostic accuracy studies using artificial intelligence. Nature Medicine. 2025. DOI:10.1038/s41591-025-03953-8.

title: STARD 2015 guidelines for reporting diagnostic accuracy studies: explanation and elaboration
authors: Jérémie F. Cohen; Daniël A. Korevaar; Douglas G. Altman; David E. Bruns; Constantine Gatsonis; Lotty Hooft; Les Irwig; Deborah Levine; et al.
research_question: How should STARD 2015 items be applied and interpreted?
method: Explanation and elaboration document with examples
major_results: Detailed item-by-item guidance for diagnostic accuracy reporting
limitations: Narrative guideline
relevance_to_project: Used to structure evaluation reporting (index test, reference standard, flow and timing)
citation: Bossuyt PMM, Reitsma JB, Bruns DE, et al. STARD 2015 explanation and elaboration. BMJ Open. 2016. DOI:10.1136/bmjopen-2016-012799.

title: The TRIPOD-LLM reporting guideline for studies using large language models
authors: Jack Gallifant; Majid Afshar; Saleem Ameen; Yindalon Aphinyanaphongs; Shan Chen; Giovanni Enrico Cacciamani; Dina Demner‐Fushman; Dmitriy Dligach; et al.
research_question: How should studies that use LLMs (prompting, agents) be reported?
method: Reporting guideline development for LLM-based health research
major_results: Specifies reporting of prompts, model versions, decoding parameters, evaluation of hallucination and consistency
limitations: New guideline; adoption still settling
relevance_to_project: Directly governs how this project reports agent prompts, model versions and run-to-run stability
citation: Gallifant J, Afshar M, Ameen S, et al. The TRIPOD-LLM reporting guideline for studies using large language models. Nature Medicine. 2025. DOI:10.1038/s41591-024-03425-5.

title: International pediatric sepsis consensus conference: Definitions for sepsis and organ dysfunction in pediatrics*
authors: Brahm Goldstein; Brett P. Giroir; Adrienne G. Randolph
research_question: What definitions of sepsis and organ dysfunction apply to pediatric patients?
method: Expert consensus (IPSCC)
major_results: Establishes pediatric-specific sepsis definitions and PRISM/PELOD organ-dysfunction context; explicitly derived from pediatric expert consensus
limitations: SIRS-based; superseded in 2024 by Phoenix criteria (retained for historical comparability)
relevance_to_project: Baseline pediatric sepsis rule set in knowledge/sepsis_rules.yaml, superseded by Phoenix where applicable
citation: Goldstein B, Giroir B, Randolph AG. International pediatric sepsis consensus conference: Definitions for sepsis and organ dysfunction in pediatrics. Pediatr Crit Care Med. 2005. DOI:10.1097/01.pcc.0000149131.72248.e6.

title: International Consensus Criteria for Pediatric Sepsis and Septic Shock
authors: Luregn Jan Schlapbach; Robert Scott Watson; Lauren R. Sorce; Andrew Charles Argent; Kusum Menon; Mark W. Hall; Samuel Akech; David J. Albers; et al.
research_question: What updated international criteria define sepsis and septic shock in children?
method: SCCM task force of 35 experts; international survey, systematic review and meta-analysis, plus organ-dysfunction score built on >3 million EHR records
major_results: Replaces the 2005 SIRS-based definitions with organ-dysfunction-based Phoenix criteria
limitations: Consensus plus retrospective EHR derivation; external validation pending for some settings
relevance_to_project: Authoritative, age-aware rule source for the high-acuity watchdog and knowledge/sepsis_rules.yaml
citation: Schlapbach LJ, Watson RS, Sorce LR, et al. International Consensus Criteria for Pediatric Sepsis and Septic Shock (Phoenix). JAMA. 2024. DOI:10.1001/jama.2024.0179.

title: Development and Validation of the Phoenix Criteria for Pediatric Sepsis and Septic Shock
authors: Lazaro Nelson Sanchez-Pinto; Tellen D. Bennett; Peter E. DeWitt; Seth Russell; Margaret N. Rebull; Blake Martin; Samuel Akech; David J. Albers; et al.
research_question: Can data-driven criteria predict mortality in children with suspected infection across settings?
method: Multicentre retrospective cohort; stacked regression models; internal and external validation in 10 health systems (US, Colombia, Bangladesh, China, Kenya)
dataset: Emergency and inpatient encounters of children <18 years, 2010-2019
major_results: Derives the Phoenix Sepsis/Septic Shock score with external validation across differently resourced settings
limitations: Retrospective EHR; variable availability differs by site; not designed for LLM agents
relevance_to_project: Quantitative source for watchdog thresholds; cited in knowledge/source_manifest.json
citation: Sanchez-Pinto LN, Bennett TD, DeWitt PE, et al. Development and Validation of the Phoenix Criteria for Pediatric Sepsis and Septic Shock. JAMA. 2024. DOI:10.1001/jama.2024.0196.

title: Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease: A Scientific Statement for Health Professionals From the American Heart Association
authors: Brian W. McCrindle; Anne Heitzman Rowley; Jane W. Newburger; Jane C. Burns; Anne F. Bolger; Michael H. Gewitz; Annette Baker; Mary Anne Jackson; et al.
research_question: What are the diagnostic criteria and management recommendations for Kawasaki disease?
method: Expert scientific statement (AHA)
major_results: Defines classic, atypical and incomplete Kawasaki disease criteria and the role of echocardiography
limitations: US-centric statement; criteria require clinical judgement
relevance_to_project: Citable criterion for the watchdog's Kawasaki rule (only when fever + compatible findings present)
citation: McCrindle BW, Rowley AH, Newburger JW, et al. Kawasaki Disease scientific statement. Circulation. 2017. DOI:10.1161/CIR.0000000000000484.

title: A practical score for the early diagnosis of acute appendicitis
authors: Alfredo Alvarado
publisher: Elsevier (for the American College of Emergency Physicians)
research_question: Can a simple weighted score from symptoms, signs and lab findings aid early appendicitis diagnosis?
method: Derivation of the Alvarado score
dataset: Emergency surgical patients evaluated for appendicitis
major_results: Provides the AS score carried in the Regensburg dataset; emphasises migration of pain, RLQ tenderness, leukocytosis
limitations: Adult-derived (originally adults); paediatric performance variable
relevance_to_project: Explains the Alvarado_Score feature and the label-circularity caveat from the audit
citation: Alvarado A. A practical score for the early diagnosis of acute appendicitis. Ann Emerg Med. 1986. DOI:10.1016/S0196-0644(86)80993-3.

title: Selective Imaging Strategies for the Diagnosis of Appendicitis in Children
authors: Barbara M. García Peña; E. Francis Cook; Kenneth D. Mandl
research_question: Which imaging strategy best supports appendicitis diagnosis in children?
method: Decision/cost-effectiveness analysis of imaging strategies in pediatric appendicitis
major_results: Structured imaging pathways can reduce unnecessary imaging while maintaining diagnostic accuracy
limitations: Modelling study; older imaging era (pre-POCUS)
relevance_to_project: Supports recommending 'information or tests' via the arbitrator rather than defaulting to imaging
citation: Horwitz MSN, Allen JR, Hout MS, et al. Selective Imaging Strategies for the Diagnosis of Appendicitis in Children. Pediatrics. 2004. DOI:10.1542/peds.113.1.24.

title: LightGBM: A Highly Efficient Gradient Boosting Decision Tree
authors: Guolin Ke; Qi Meng; Thomas Finley; Taifeng Wang; Wei Chen; Weidong Ma; Qiwei Ye; Tie-Yan Liu
journal_or_conference: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30 (NeurIPS)
research_question: How can gradient boosting be scaled to large datasets with low memory?
method: Algorithm design: histogram-based gradient boosting with leaf-wise growth and feature bundling
major_results: Leaf-wise boosting with GOSS/EFB gives large speed and memory gains at comparable accuracy
limitations: Not medical; does not address calibration (post-hoc calibration still required)
relevance_to_project: Primary ML algorithm for the tabular prediction layer
citation: Ke G, Meng Q, Finley T, et al. LightGBM: A Highly Efficient Gradient Boosting Decision Tree. NeurIPS 2017. URL:https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2017/hash/6449f44a102fde848669bdd9eb6b76fa-Abstract.html.

title: Balancing Interpretability and Accuracy: A Comparative Evaluation of Logistic Regression and Machine Learning Approaches for Coronary Heart Disease Risk Prediction in Low-Resource Settings
authors: Maurice Wanyonyi; Zakayo Ndiku Morris; Faith Mueni Musyoka; Dominic Makaa Kitavi
journal_or_conference: IAENG International Journal of Computer Science
database/index: IAENG (publisher-verified via issue index; Scopus-indexed journal)
research_question: How do interpretable models compare with more accurate ML models for clinical risk prediction in low-resource settings?
method: Comparative evaluation of logistic regression vs machine learning classifiers
dataset: Clinical risk-prediction dataset for coronary heart disease (see paper)
major_results: Reports the interpretability/accuracy trade-off empirically; interpretable models can rival ML on tabular clinical risk
limitations: Non-pediatric domain; journal article without DOI
relevance_to_project: Serves the requested IAENG source category and supports retaining an interpretable baseline alongside LightGBM
citation: Wanyonyi M, Morris ZN, Musyoka FM, Kitavi DM. Balancing Interpretability and Accuracy... IAENG Int J Comput Sci. 2026;53(3):1135-1154. URL:https://www.iaeng.org/IJCS/issues_v53/issue_3/IJCS_53_3_19.pdf
